title: The Application and Ethical Implication of Generative AI in Mental Health: Systematic Review
study_design: Systematic review following PRISMA 2020; literature search across PubMed, ACM Digital Library, Scopus, Embase, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed studies published from October 1, 2019, to September 30, 2024
population: Peer-reviewed original research studies on generative AI applications in mental health, covering diagnosis and assessment, therapeutic tools, and clinician support; included studies involved general populations, vulnerable groups, patients, clinicians, social media users, and simulated clinical cases
country_or_setting: Global/multinational literature across mental health care, digital health, social media, and clinical/educational settings
ai_type_application: Generative AI, primarily large language models and conversational agents/chatbots used for mental health diagnosis and assessment, therapeutic support, and clinician assistance
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure to or implementation of GenAI systems such as GPT-series, LLaMA, Gemini, Falcon, Mistral, Flan-T5 and related prompt-engineered, fine-tuned, hybrid, or retrieval-augmented models for mental health tasks
comparator_control_group: Varied across included studies; comparators included traditional machine learning models, pretrained language models such as BERT, human clinicians/experts, primary care physicians, or no explicit comparator
mental_health_outcome: Depression, suicide risk/suicidality, anxiety, stress, emotion recognition/regulation, obsessive-compulsive disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, PTSD, mental resilience, mindfulness, problematic smartphone use, preoperative anxiety, relationship distress, and general emotional support outcomes
outcome_measurement_tool: Varied by included study; included accuracy, precision, balanced accuracy, correlations with expert ratings, psychometric instruments such as State-Trait Anxiety Inventory and Self-Efficacy Scale, user satisfaction/engagement metrics, qualitative interviews, expert review, perplexity, BLEU, top-k accuracy, and reporting quality assessed in this review using MI-CLAIM-GEN
positive_effects: GenAI showed promise in enhancing diagnostic accuracy, especially for suicide risk and depression detection; multimodal approaches improved detection reliability; therapeutic chatbots were often associated with emotional relief, perceived empathy, self-reflection, reduced anxiety, reduced problematic smartphone use, and increased intervention acceptance; clinician-support applications may reduce administrative burden, assist treatment planning, case formulation, psychoeducation, training, and documentation
negative_effects_harms: Ethical and practical risks included privacy and data security concerns, algorithmic bias and fairness issues, reduced performance across dialectal/cultural contexts, hallucinations and medically inaccurate content, incorrect suicide-related documentation, inconsistent responses, insufficient crisis detection and intervention, overtrust in AI, abrupt termination of high-risk conversations, generic or repetitive advice, limited personalization, and lack of governance/oversight
evidence_type: Systematic review of 79 peer-reviewed original studies with mixed evidence including experimental studies, randomized controlled trials, quasi-experiments, simulated evaluations, retrospective analyses, qualitative studies, and technical benchmark studies
main_finding: Generative AI shows substantial potential as a complementary tool in mental health diagnosis, therapeutic support, and clinician assistance, but current evidence is dominated by proof-of-concept and simulated studies, with limited real-world deployment and major ethical concerns around privacy, fairness, safety, and governance
effect_size_key_result: Among reviewed studies, GPT-4 achieved precision up to 0.96 for suicidal risk prediction in some studies; depression detection accuracy reached 0.902 using semistructured diaries in one study; multimodal prompting for passive sensing depression classification achieved up to 61.1% accuracy; a 5-week field study reported 7% to 10% reduction in smartphone use and up to 22.5% improvement in intervention acceptance; overall reporting transparency averaged 45.39% yes on MI-CLAIM-GEN items
limitations_bias: Heterogeneity in study designs, datasets, and evaluation metrics prevented meta-analysis; most included studies focused on proof-of-concept or simulated interactions rather than real-world or longitudinal deployment; evidence largely centered on text-based language models; reliance on social media data may bias samples toward younger, digitally active, English-speaking users; reporting quality was moderate with poor reproducibility, limited harm assessment, limited real-world evaluation, and underreporting of data representativeness and resources
relevance_to_our_review: Highly relevant as a broad synthesis of how AI, specifically generative AI, affects mental health through diagnostic, therapeutic, and clinician-support applications, including both beneficial and harmful effects
reason_for_decision: Directly addresses AI effects on mental health across multiple application domains and synthesizes positive outcomes, harms, and ethical implications from 79 studies
notes_for_research_question: Useful umbrella source for identifying both beneficial and adverse mental health effects of generative AI. However, because it is a review and not a single primary causal study, causal inference is limited and real-world outcome evidence remains weak. Includes strong discussion of risks such as bias, hallucination, crisis-management failures, and privacy harms.
